x: The Lok Sabha's maximum strength under Article 81 is 552: up to 530 from the States and up to 20 from the Union Territories. 543 is its present elected strength, not the maximum.
t: Discriminate maximum strength (552) from present strength (543) and the States' share (530).

x: Option C is the incorrect statement. A Lok Sabha candidate must be registered as a voter in any parliamentary constituency, not an Assembly constituency. The citizenship and minimum-age-25 conditions are correct.
t: Check which constituency type the voter-registration condition names.

x: Both are true: the Lok Sabha's normal term is five years from its first sitting, and the President can dissolve it earlier. Early dissolution is an exception to the term, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether R gives the reason for A or only an exception to it.

x: Both are true. The 104th Amendment (2019) ended the nomination of two Anglo-Indians under Article 331 from 25 January 2020, and extended SC/ST seat reservation till 2030.
t: Recall the two changes made by the 104th Amendment together.

x: Article 81 covers composition, 83 duration, 84 qualifications and 330 SC/ST reservation, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Fix Article 81 (composition) and 330 (reservation) first, then place 83 and 84.

x: All four are correct: the Speaker decides Tenth Schedule disqualifications, a member of both Houses must choose within 10 days, a non-member Minister must be elected within six months, and the ministry is capped at 15% of the Lok Sabha.
t: Check each number: 10 days, six months, 15 per cent.

x: All four vacate a Lok Sabha seat: resignation to the Speaker, disqualification, absence for 60 days without permission, and election to the other House.
t: Recall the vacancy grounds and the 60-day absence rule.

x: All four are correct. A candidate must not hold an office of profit, be of unsound mind or be an undischarged insolvent, and further qualifications are prescribed by the Representation of the People Act.
t: Check each condition against the Lok Sabha qualification list.

x: Option C is incorrect: Article 102 deals with disqualifications, not qualifications (those are in Article 84). Disqualifications also come from the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
t: Discriminate qualifications (Article 84) from disqualifications (Article 102).

x: A is true: during a National Emergency, Parliament can extend the Lok Sabha's term by one year at a time. R is false, because the extension is by Parliament, not the President, and not by two years.
t: Check both who extends the term and by how long.

x: All three are correct: Lok Sabha seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to their population, and the reservation was first given for ten years.
t: Recall the basis (population) and the original duration (ten years).

x: The quorum of the Lok Sabha is one-tenth of its total membership. One-fifth and one-third are distractors.
t: Recall the quorum fraction for either House of Parliament.

x: Present elected strength 543, Union Territory members 13, first Lok Sabha 489, Uttar Pradesh 80, so the answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Match the biggest number (543) first, then 489, 80 and 13.

x: All three are correct: Article 102 covers Lok Sabha disqualifications, Article 331 covered the now-discontinued Anglo-Indian nomination, and Article 326 provides adult suffrage.
t: Recall the subject of each Article number.

x: Under the Representation of the People Act, a person can contest from at most two constituencies at a time.
t: Recall the limit on constituencies a candidate may contest.

x: The Rajya Sabha's maximum strength under Article 80 is 250: up to 238 elected representatives of States and UTs plus 12 nominated members. 245 is its present strength.
t: Discriminate maximum (250 = 238 + 12) from present strength (245).

x: Option A is incorrect: a Rajya Sabha member must be at least 30 years old. 25 years is the minimum age for the Lok Sabha.
t: Discriminate the minimum ages for the Lok Sabha (25) and Rajya Sabha (30).

x: Both are true: under Article 249, the Rajya Sabha can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest, by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. R states the procedure for that power.
t: Recall Article 249 and its majority requirement.

x: Article 80 covers composition, 83(1) the Rajya Sabha as a permanent House, 84 qualifications, and the Fourth Schedule the allocation of seats, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Place the Fourth Schedule (seat allocation) first, then the Articles.

x: I and II are correct: the Rajya Sabha is elected indirectly by elected MLAs through proportional representation by single transferable vote. III is false because it is a permanent House and is never dissolved.
t: Find the statement that contradicts the Rajya Sabha being a permanent House.

x: Both are true. Among the Union Territories, only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir are represented in the Rajya Sabha, and its quorum, like the Lok Sabha's, is one-tenth of total membership.
t: Recall the three UTs with Rajya Sabha seats and the quorum fraction.

x: A Rajya Sabha member resigns to the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, who is the Vice-President. Lok Sabha members resign to the Speaker.
t: Discriminate the resignation authority for each House.

x: The Rajya Sabha has 245 members at present: 233 elected and 12 nominated. 250 and 238 are the maximum limits, not the present figures.
t: Discriminate present figures (245, 233) from maximum limits (250, 238).

x: Rajya Sabha seats are allocated among States on the basis of population, so States do not get equal representation as in the US Senate.
t: Recall the basis of seat allocation in the Fourth Schedule.

x: The President nominates 12 members with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service. Each field matches its own description, so the answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each field to its same-named description.

x: Both are true: a Rajya Sabha member must not hold an office of profit, and the other disqualifications are the same as for the Lok Sabha under Article 102, the RP Act, 1951 and the Tenth Schedule.
t: Recall that disqualification rules are common to both Houses.

x: All three are correct: a Rajya Sabha member serves six years, about one-third retire every two years, and a casual vacancy is filled only for the rest of the term.
t: Check the six-year term, two-year retirement cycle and casual-vacancy rule.

x: Both are true: under Article 312, the Rajya Sabha can start the creation of a new All-India Service, by a two-thirds majority. The majority is a procedure, not the reason the power exists, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a voting requirement can explain why a power exists.

x: All three are correct: the Rajya Sabha has equal powers in Constitutional Amendment Bills and can introduce both Ordinary and Constitutional Amendment Bills. Its powers are restricted only for Money Bills.
t: Remember that only Money Bills limit the Rajya Sabha's role.

x: All four are correct: the minimum age is 25, the maximum strength 552, election is direct, and the term is five years.
t: Check each Lok Sabha number: 25, 552 and five years.

x: Only three statements are listed and all three are true: the Lok Sabha can be dissolved, it has no nominated members, and the Anglo-Indian nomination has ended. "All four" is impossible.
t: Count the listed statements before choosing a count option.

x: Option D is incorrect. A Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, which also has the final say; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days.
t: Discriminate the roles of the two Houses on Money Bills.

x: Both are true: the Lok Sabha introduces Money Bills and has the final say, and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days. The Rajya Sabha's limited role is why the Lok Sabha's word is final, so R explains A.
t: Ask whether R's limit on one House accounts for A's power of the other.

x: Nargis Dutt, nominated in 1980, was the first nominated woman member. Uttar Pradesh has the most Rajya Sabha seats (31), and the Chairman decides anti-defection questions, so the answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Match the person and year first, then the State and the authority.

x: Statement A is true: Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. B is false: the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha but not a constituent part or member of Parliament.
t: Discriminate between presiding over a House and being part of Parliament.

x: The Union Council of Ministers is under Article 74, the State Council under Article 163, the Council of States under Article 80, and the Legislative Council under Articles 168, 169 and 171, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Pair the Union and State versions: 74 with 163, and 80 with 168 to 171.

x: Both are true: Article 75(3) makes the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, which explains A. It is not responsible to the Rajya Sabha or to Parliament as a whole.
t: Recall Article 75(3) and which House it names.

x: Option B is incorrect. Union Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, not the Prime Minister. State Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure, not the Chief Minister's.
t: Discriminate the formal head (President, Governor) from the political head.

x: All three are correct: the 91st Amendment, 2003 caps the Union ministry at 15% of the Lok Sabha and a State ministry at 15% of the Assembly, and a State ministry must have at least 12 Ministers.
t: Recall the 91st Amendment's 15 per cent cap and the minimum of 12.

x: Under Article 75(5), a non-member can be a Union Minister for at most six consecutive months. The same six-month limit applies to State Ministers under Article 164(4).
t: Recall the six-month window for non-member Ministers.

x: Both are true: the Cabinet is the smaller inner core of the Council of Ministers, and the word 'Cabinet' entered the Constitution only through Article 352, by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
t: Recall the one Article and amendment that bring the word 'Cabinet' in.

x: Both are true: the 44th Amendment, 1978 lets the President return ministerial advice once for reconsideration, but the advice binds after that. This rule is exactly why the President is bound, so R explains A.
t: Recall the 42nd and 44th Amendment changes to Article 74.

x: Option C is incorrect: a member of the Council of States serves six years, not five. It is a permanent House in which one-third of the members retire every two years, and the minimum age is 30.
t: Discriminate the six-year Rajya Sabha term from the five-year Lok Sabha term.

x: The Rajya Sabha's maximum strength is 250, made up of 238 from States and UTs and 12 nominated members, and the minimum age is 30, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Match the numbers knowing 250 = 238 + 12.

x: I, II and IV are correct: elected MLAs choose State representatives by proportional representation using single transferable vote, by secret ballot. III is false because nominated MLAs cannot vote.
t: Find the statement about nominated MLAs, the usual trap.

x: Both are true: under Article 169, Parliament acts only after the Assembly passes a special-majority resolution (a majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting), and then passes the law by simple majority. R explains A.
t: Recall the two steps of Article 169 and the majority each needs.

x: Option B is incorrect: under Article 171, a Legislative Council can have at most one-third of the Assembly's strength, not one-half, and at least 40 members.
t: Recall the one-third ceiling and 40-member floor of Article 171.

x: One-third is elected by MLAs and one-third by local authorities, one-twelfth each by graduates and teachers, and one-sixth is nominated by the Governor, so the answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Check that the fractions add up to one: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/6.

x: Both are true: the Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for at most four months (three months the first time, one month the second), so it cannot block the Bill permanently. R explains A.
t: Recall the 3 + 1 month delay limit of the Council.

x: The Assembly is the Lower or Popular House and is presided over by the Speaker. The Council is the Upper House or House of Elders and is presided over by the Chairman. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Pair each House with its nickname and presiding officer.

x: Article 163 provides for a State Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, like Article 74 for the President. Article 164 deals with appointment of Ministers.
t: Discriminate the Union and State parallels: 74 with 163, 75 with 164.

x: Both are true: the Governor is bound by ministerial advice, except in discretionary areas. R is an exception that limits A, not its reason, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether R explains A or only limits it.

x: Elected MLAs are the electors, the method is proportional representation by single transferable vote, voting is by secret ballot, and nominated MLAs cannot vote, so the answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Match the voters first, then the method and ballot.

x: Option C is incorrect: one-sixth of Council members are nominated by the Governor, not elected. Graduates and teachers (with three years' standing) each elect one-twelfth, and local authorities include municipalities and district boards.
t: Check the verb in each statement: elected or nominated.

x: In a State Legislature, the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill, and the Speaker's decision is final. Neither the Governor nor the Council Chairman decides.
t: Recall who certifies a Money Bill in a State.

x: Three are correct: the Assembly is the Lower or Popular House, it can be dissolved, and its term is five years. Statement 4 is false because its minimum age is 25; 30 applies to the Council.
t: Discriminate the Assembly's minimum age (25) from the Council's (30).

x: The Assembly is the dissolvable House and the Council the permanent body; the Speaker presides over the Assembly and the Chairman over the Council. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Pair each House with its permanence and presiding officer.

x: I, II and III are correct: a Money Bill starts only in the Assembly, which has the final say, while the Council can only make recommendations. IV is false because the Council can hold a Money Bill for at most 14 days, not a month.
t: Discriminate the 14-day Money Bill limit from the ordinary-Bill delays.

x: Both are true: the Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council from literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service. The fields do not explain why the share is one-sixth, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a list of fields can explain a fraction.

x: Both are true: like Rajya Sabha members, Legislative Council members serve six-year terms, and the Council is presided over by a Chairman.
t: Recall the six-year Council term and its presiding officer.

x: Both are true: Article 164(2) makes the State Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly, which is what A states. R explains A.
t: Recall Article 164(2), the State parallel of Article 75(3).

x: Part VI, Articles 168–212, covers State Legislatures. Part V, Articles 79–122, covers Parliament.
t: Discriminate Part V (Union) from Part VI (States).

x: Both are true: under Article 168, a bicameral State Legislature has the Governor, Assembly and Council, and a unicameral one has the Governor and Assembly. The Governor is part of both.
t: Remember that the Governor is part of every State Legislature.

x: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats, among the six bicameral States.
t: Recall the largest of the six State Legislative Councils.

x: The Government of India Act, 1919 first brought bicameralism to the Centre, with the Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly. The 1935 Act brought it to some provinces.
t: Discriminate the 1919 Act (Centre) from the 1935 Act (provinces).

x: The Legislative Council is under Article 171, the Council of States under Article 80, the Legislative Assembly under Article 170, and State Legislatures as a whole under Articles 168–212, so the answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Discriminate Article 170 (Assembly) from 171 (Council).

x: Option B is incorrect. The Council is permanent, so it cannot be dissolved, but it can be abolished under Article 169. One-third of its members retire every two years.
t: Discriminate between dissolving a House and abolishing it.

x: All three are correct: a Council can have at most one-third of the Assembly's strength and at least 40 members, and an Assembly has at most 500 and at least 60 members.
t: Recall the four limits: 1/3, 40, 500 and 60.

x: Under Article 182, the Council elects its Chairman from among its own members. The Governor does not nominate the Chairman, and the Vice-President chairs only the Rajya Sabha.
t: Discriminate the Council's Chairman from the Rajya Sabha's ex-officio Chairman.

x: Both are true: Parliament passes the law by simple majority, and the Constitution itself says such a law is not an amendment under Article 368. R explains how the law is passed, not why it is excluded from Article 368.
t: Ask whether the type of majority explains the Article 368 exclusion.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Assembly's resolution is only a request and does not legally compel the Union Government to bring a Bill. It does need a special majority (50% of total membership and two-thirds present and voting).
t: Look for the statement that makes a recommendation binding.

x: Council elections use proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot, as Rajya Sabha elections do. First-past-the-post and open ballot are distractors.
t: Recall that indirect elections use the single transferable vote.

x: Five fields are valid: literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service. Industrial activity is not one of them.
t: Add the co-operative movement to the Rajya Sabha's four fields.

x: Option B is incorrect: commerce is not a field for nomination to the Council. The five fields are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service.
t: Check each field against the five Article 171 fields.

x: Under Article 198, a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Legislative Assembly, never in the Council.
t: Recall the State parallel of the Lok Sabha's Money Bill rule.

x: Both are true: the Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill and must return it within 14 days. If it does not, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
t: Recall the 14-day limit and the deemed-passed rule.

x: I and II are correct: the Council can delay an ordinary Bill for three months, then one month after it is passed again. III is false because the Council has no veto.
t: Find the statement giving the Council a veto.

x: A State Legislative Council, though permanent, can be abolished under Article 169. The Rajya Sabha cannot be abolished, which is the difference.
t: Discriminate abolition of the State Council from the permanence of the Rajya Sabha.

x: Andhra Pradesh is one of the six bicameral States, along with Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh. Gujarat, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu are unicameral.
t: Recall the six States that have Legislative Councils.

x: Both are true: the Legislative Council is a permanent body, and the Assembly has a five-year term unless it is dissolved earlier.
t: Discriminate the permanent Council from the dissolvable Assembly.

x: The State Legislative Council is presided over by its Chairman, the Council of States by the Vice-President, and the Assembly by the Speaker, so the answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
t: Match each House to its presiding officer.

x: All three are correct: the minimum age is 25 for the Assembly and 30 for both the Legislative Council and the Council of States.
t: Remember that both Upper Houses require age 30.

x: Both are true: the graduates who elect one-twelfth of the Council must have at least three years' standing and must live in the State.
t: Recall the two conditions on the graduates' constituency.

x: Both are true: teachers who elect one-twelfth of the Council must have three years' standing and teach in institutions of at least secondary-school level.
t: Recall the teaching level and years of standing.

x: Both are true: the Council receives a Money Bill only for recommendations, so the Assembly is free to accept or reject them. R explains A.
t: Ask whether a purely recommendatory role explains the Assembly's freedom.

x: Article 198 sets out the special procedure for Money Bills in a State Legislature. Article 169 is about creating or abolishing Councils and Article 171 about their composition.
t: Recall Article 198, the State parallel of Article 109.

x: The Legislative Council and the Council of States both have six-year terms with one-third retiring every two years. The Assembly has a five-year term unless dissolved earlier, so the answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Match the odd one out, the five-year Assembly, first.

x: All four are bicameral: Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra and Karnataka. With Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, they make up the six.
t: Check each State against the six with Legislative Councils.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council, not one-fourth. Local authorities and MLAs each elect one-third, and MLAs choose from among non-members.
t: Recall the Governor's share: one-sixth.

x: Both are true: the Assembly is temporary because its normal term is five years and it can be dissolved earlier. R explains A.
t: Ask whether a fixed, dissolvable term explains being temporary.

x: A is true: the co-operative movement is a nomination field for the State Legislative Council. B is false: under Article 80, the Rajya Sabha's fields are only literature, science, art and social service.
t: Discriminate the Council's five fields from the Rajya Sabha's four.

x: The State Legislative Council is under Article 171, the Council of States under Article 80, and the Legislative Assembly under Article 170, so the answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
t: Discriminate Article 170 (Assembly) from 171 (Council).

x: Option D is incorrect: the Council has no veto and cannot block an ordinary Bill for good. It can delay the Bill for three months, then one month after it is passed again, four months in all.
t: Look for the statement giving the Council a veto.

x: All four are correct: the Assembly is the Lower House and the Council the Upper House, the Assembly cannot be abolished (only the Council can), and the Council of States has at most 250 members.
t: Discriminate which State House can be abolished.

x: Both are true: the Vice-President chairs the Council of States ex officio without being a member. Being a non-member Chairman is exactly what makes the Vice-President not a member, so R explains A.
t: Ask whether R's non-member status explains A.

x: Two are local authorities: municipalities and district boards. Graduates and teachers are separate electorates, each electing one-twelfth of the Council.
t: Discriminate local authorities from the graduates' and teachers' electorates.
